name: Vimalakirti
role: Wise lay disciple in a famous Mahayana sutra
summary: Vimalakirti is the wise layman of Vaishali at the centre of the Vimalakirti Sutra, a Mahayana text. He is shown teaching monks and bodhisattvas, and even the Buddha's great disciples, without being a monk.
about: Vimalakirti is the central figure of the Vimalakirti Sutra, a Mahayana text that portrays him as a rich Licchavi householder in Vaishali, in present-day Bihar, and a contemporary of the Buddha. The sutra says that he is a master of skilful means who speaks with respect to everyone but is not overawed even by the Buddha's great disciples. Scholars disagree whether he was a historical person; many see him as a literary figure, while traditional scholars treat him as real. Translator Burton Watson dates the sutra to around 100 CE. The sutra's best-known scenes show his debate with Manjushri, a goddess scattering flowers, and his famous silence on the teaching of non-duality.
kidSummary: Vimalakirti was a wise and rich man from Vaishali who was not a monk. The sutra says he knew so much about kindness and wisdom that monks and bodhisattvas came to learn from him. His house had a magic trick: it stayed small outside, but made room for crowds.

story.title: A wise householder
story.text: The Vimalakirti Sutra says Vimalakirti was a rich man in Vaishali who lived an ordinary home life but understood deep truths.

story.title: A visit to his bedside
story.text: In the sutra, Vimalakirti falls ill and the Buddha sends his disciples to ask about him. Many say they are afraid to go because he once corrected them.

story.title: Manjushri arrives
story.text: Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, goes at last. Thousands follow, and Vimalakirti's small room somehow holds them all.

story.title: Flowers on the monks
story.text: A goddess in the room scatters flowers. They stick to the monks, who are still holding on to ideas, but slip off the bodhisattvas.

story.title: The great silence
story.text: Asked about the truth beyond opposites, Vimalakirti answers with silence. Manjushri praises it as the best answer.

teaches: Wisdom can live in an ordinary home

facts.text: In chapter 2 the sutra shows the rich householder visiting gambling halls, brothels and the haunts of rival philosophers, using each place to guide people.
In chapter 3, the Buddha's great disciples all refuse to visit the sick Vimalakirti because each was once outdone by him; he beat Sariputra by arguing that true meditation is not just sitting still.
In the 7th century, the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang reported being shown the house site said to be Vimalakirti's at Vaishali; Wang Xuance also described visiting.
In Chinese Chan monasteries, the word for abbot, fangzhang, refers to the ten-foot-square stone room attributed to Vimalakirti.
A commentary on the sutra, the Yuimagyo gisho, is attributed to Prince Shotoku (574-622), making it one of the earliest works of Japanese Buddhism.
In chapter 1 five hundred Licchavi youths each offer the Buddha a parasol, and he turns them into one giant parasol that covers the whole universe.
In chapter 6 the goddess has lived in his room for twelve years; Sariputra tries to shake the clinging flowers off with supernatural powers and fails, and she tells him he still holds a shallow view.
A Sanskrit manuscript of the sutra was found in the Potala Palace in Lhasa in 1999, published in 2004, and a critical edition followed in 2006.
In chapter 8, after the bodhisattvas speak about non-duality and Manjushri says that explaining it already falls into duality, Vimalakirti replies with silence.
Also in chapter 1, the Buddha says a Buddha-field is pure when the mind is pure. Sariputra cannot see this at first, so the Buddha briefly shows him the purity.

In chapter 5 Vimalakirti summons 32,000 huge lion thrones from a distant Buddha-field without enlarging his small room. The seats are so tall that advanced bodhisattvas must stretch their bodies to about 42,000 yojanas to sit on them.
The Tang poet Wang Wei took his courtesy name from Vimalakirti, a sign of how deeply the sutra mattered to Chinese writers.
Wikipedia shows a Tang-dynasty painting from the Dunhuang caves of Vimalakirti debating Manjushri, so the sickroom duel was a favourite subject of cave painters on the Silk Road.
Dunhuang also yielded Chinese copies of the sutra, and some fragments were written on the back of an Old Tibetan Chronicle, so the sutra shared a page with a very different book.
In the sutra, Vimalakirti pretends to be ill so that people will come to see him, and he uses every sympathy visit to teach.
In Zen, chapter 8's non-duality scene became case 84 of the Hekiganroku, a famous koan collection, and later Chan teachers took Vimalakirti's silence as a sign that truth lies beyond words.
In chapter 6, when Sariputra asks the goddess why she still has a woman's body, she swaps bodies with him; he cannot change back until she lets him.
In chapter 9, a bodhisattva conjured by Vimalakirti fetches fragrant food from a far-off Buddha-world, and a single bowl feeds the whole assembly.
In chapter 10, Vimalakirti lifts the entire assembly in one hand and carries it to Amrapali's garden, where the Buddha is teaching.
The Longmen Grottoes in China hold a stone relief of Vimalakirti, and the Hossō temple Kofuku-ji in Japan has a figure of Layman Yuima, as his name is said in Japanese.
Wikipedia also records a Southern Song silk painting of Vimalakirti in the Kyoto National Museum, showing how far the layman's image travelled from Vaishali to Japan.

quiz.q: What famous answer did Vimalakirti give about the truth beyond opposites?
quiz.why: The sutra says he answered with silence.

quiz.q: In which city did Vimalakirti live, according to the sutra?
quiz.why: He was a Licchavi layman of Vaishali.

quiz.q: Which bodhisattva visits him in the sutra?
quiz.why: Manjushri goes to ask after his health and debates him.

quiz.q: What happens to the flowers the goddess scatters?
quiz.why: They cling to the monks but fall off the bodhisattvas.
